nodes.label: Characters and bytes
nodes.body: Characters and bytes is the branch on what a character actually is underneath the string notation: a number in the Unicode standard, and the rules for turning a sequence of those numbers into the bytes a file or a network connection actually stores and sends (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Characters and bytes is the branch on what a character actually is underneath the string notation: a number in the Unicode standard, and the rules for turning a sequence of those numbers into the bytes a file or a network connection actually stores and sends (Sweigart, 2025).

Code point conversion covers ord() and chr(), which move between a character and its number directly. Text encodings covers the broader question of turning a whole string into bytes and back, the errors that can happen along the way, and how a text file's encoding is chosen.

nodes.label: Code point conversion
nodes.body: Every character that Python can represent has a number assigned to it by the Unicode standard, called its code point, running from 0 up to 0x10FFFF (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Every character that Python can represent has a number assigned to it by the Unicode standard, called its code point, running from 0 up to 0x10FFFF (Sweigart, 2025).

ord and chr is the one concept in this subsection: ord() reads a single character and gives back its code point, and chr() does the reverse, taking a code point and giving back the one-character string it names.

nodes.label: Ord and chr
nodes.body: ord() takes a one-character string and returns its code point as a plain integer; chr() takes an integer code point and returns the single character it names. ord('A') is 65, ord('4') is 52 and ord('!') is 33; chr(65) is 'A', and since code points for letters of the same case run in order, chr(ord('A') + 1) is 'B' and ord('A') < ord('B') is True (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: ord() takes a one-character string and returns its code point as a plain integer; chr() takes an integer code point and returns the single character it names. ord('A') is 65, ord('4') is 52 and ord('!') is 33; chr(65) is 'A', and since code points for letters of the same case run in order, chr(ord('A') + 1) is 'B' and ord('A') < ord('B') is True (Sweigart, 2025).

The same two functions work identically outside the ASCII range that the chapter's own examples stay inside: the code point of the euro sign is 8364, so ord('\u20ac') is 8364 and chr(8364) == '\u20ac' is True; the snake emoji has the much larger code point 128013, so ord('\U0001f40d') is 128013 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

chr() only accepts a value from 0 to 0x10FFFF inclusive, the full range Unicode defines, and raises ValueError for anything outside it, since there is no character for it to name; ord() only accepts a string of exactly one character and raises TypeError for a longer one, since a longer string would have more than one code point to report.

nodes.definition: Every character has a Unicode code point, an integer from 0 to 0x10FFFF; ord() gives the code point of a one-character string and chr() gives the character of a code point, so ord('A') is 65 and chr(ord('A') + 1) is 'B'.

nodes.label: Text encodings
nodes.body: Encoding turns a string of characters into a sequence of bytes using a chosen set of rules, and decoding reverses the same rules to turn bytes back into a string; the two sides of the pair must agree on the same encoding or the text comes back wrong (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Encoding turns a string of characters into a sequence of bytes using a chosen set of rules, and decoding reverses the same rules to turn bytes back into a string; the two sides of the pair must agree on the same encoding or the text comes back wrong (Sweigart, 2025).

Utf8 encoding covers the one encoding the chapter recommends by name and the arithmetic of how many bytes a character takes. Encode decode errors covers what happens, and what can be done, when a character cannot be represented or bytes cannot be read back as valid text. File encoding covers the encoding a text file is read and written with, and what Python assumes when none is named.

nodes.label: Utf8 encoding
nodes.body: In the UTF-8 encoding, each character takes between one and four bytes depending on its code point, so a string's length in characters and its length in bytes need not match. 'caf\xe9'.encode('utf-8') gives b'caf\xc3\xa9': the four characters c, a, f and the accented e become five bytes, because the accented e alone takes two bytes while the three plain ASCII letters each take one (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Decoding those same bytes with .decode('utf-8') returns the original four-character string exactly.

paras.text: In the UTF-8 encoding, each character takes between one and four bytes depending on its code point, so a string's length in characters and its length in bytes need not match. 'caf\xe9'.encode('utf-8') gives b'caf\xc3\xa9': the four characters c, a, f and the accented e become five bytes, because the accented e alone takes two bytes while the three plain ASCII letters each take one (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Decoding those same bytes with .decode('utf-8') returns the original four-character string exactly.

The gap between character count and byte count can be larger still: the snake emoji is one character, yet it takes four bytes in UTF-8, and, separately, also four bytes in UTF-16, two different encodings arriving at the same byte count for different reasons bound up in how each one represents code points outside the earliest part of Unicode.

The chapter states plainly that 'utf-8' is the right choice about 99 percent of the time a program needs to pick an encoding, and points a curious reader toward Ned Batchelder's conference talk on the subject and a Computerphile video on character encoding for the fuller history and reasoning (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.definition: Encoding turns text into bytes and decoding turns bytes back into text; in UTF-8 a character takes one to four bytes, so a string of four characters can be five bytes long, and encode() and decode() must use the same encoding.

nodes.label: Encode decode errors
nodes.body: Encoding fails when the target encoding has no way to represent one of the characters: encoding 'caf\xe9' as 'ascii' raises UnicodeEncodeError: 'ascii' codec can't encode character '\xe9' in position 3, because ASCII has no code for the accented e at all (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Decoding can fail in the matching way when the bytes do not form valid text under the encoding named: decoding the truncated bytes b'caf\xc3' as 'utf-8' raises UnicodeDecodeError, since \xc3 alone is the first byte of a two-byte UTF-8 character whose second byte is missing.

paras.text: Encoding fails when the target encoding has no way to represent one of the characters: encoding 'caf\xe9' as 'ascii' raises UnicodeEncodeError: 'ascii' codec can't encode character '\xe9' in position 3, because ASCII has no code for the accented e at all (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Decoding can fail in the matching way when the bytes do not form valid text under the encoding named: decoding the truncated bytes b'caf\xc3' as 'utf-8' raises UnicodeDecodeError, since \xc3 alone is the first byte of a two-byte UTF-8 character whose second byte is missing.

Both encode() and decode() accept an errors argument that names a different way to handle the failure instead of raising an exception. Encoding 'caf\xe9' with errors='replace' gives b'caf?', substituting a question mark for the character that cannot be represented; errors='backslashreplace' gives b'caf\\xe9', spelling the character out as an escape sequence instead of dropping it; and errors='ignore' gives b'caf', simply leaving the unrepresentable character out.

A decoding call can also fail silently rather than raising anything: bytes that are valid under one encoding may also be valid, and wrong, under another. The UTF-8 bytes b'caf\xc3\xa9' decode without error under 'latin-1' as well, but give the wrong five-character text rather than the intended four-character word, because latin-1 reads every byte as one character instead of recognising the two-byte UTF-8 sequence. The chapter, read as printed, does not present any of these error cases.

nodes.definition: A character the encoding cannot represent raises UnicodeEncodeError and bytes that do not form valid text raise UnicodeDecodeError, unless the errors argument names another handler such as replace, backslashreplace or ignore; decoding with the wrong encoding can succeed and give wrong text.

nodes.label: File encoding
nodes.body: A text file is, underneath, a sequence of bytes, and some encoding is always used to turn the text a program writes into those bytes and back; writing 'caf\xe9' through a text wrapper set to encoding='utf-8' leaves exactly b'caf\xc3\xa9' in the underlying bytes, the same bytes the earlier concept's encode() call produced directly.

paras.text: A text file is, underneath, a sequence of bytes, and some encoding is always used to turn the text a program writes into those bytes and back; writing 'caf\xe9' through a text wrapper set to encoding='utf-8' leaves exactly b'caf\xc3\xa9' in the underlying bytes, the same bytes the earlier concept's encode() call produced directly.

open() called without naming an encoding does not fail, but it does not necessarily agree with the program that wrote the file either: it falls back to the locale's own encoding under Python 3.14.4, so a file written as UTF-8 and then read back by a separate process running under the plain C locale, with Python's UTF-8 mode switched off, was read under the ASCII codec instead and raised UnicodeDecodeError, while the identical read with encoding='utf-8' named explicitly succeeded and returned the correct text (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

PEP 686 makes UTF-8 mode the default behaviour from Python 3.15 onward, which will close most of this gap for future versions, though code written for the versions before it still needs encoding='utf-8' stated explicitly to be safe everywhere it runs (Inada, 2022). The chapter, read as printed, mentions files only as the place where encoding eventually matters and does not go into open()'s own default.

nodes.definition: A text file is turned into bytes by an encoding; open() called without one uses the locale encoding in Python 3.14, which is why a program should name encoding='utf-8' when it writes or reads text it means to share.

nodes.body: Clipboard and programs is the chapter's closing branch: the third-party module that lets a program read from and write to the operating system's clipboard, and the chapter's own small programs, which put the rest of the chapter's string operations to work on real text (Sweigart, 2025).

Clipboard programs covers the pyperclip module itself. Project programs covers the bullet-point adder, the alternating-case program, the input-validation functions, the Pig Latin translator and the practice table printer, one after another in the chapter's own order.

nodes.label: Clipboard programs
nodes.body: The operating system's clipboard lets one program hand a block of text to another without a file in between, and the chapter uses it as the way its small programs receive and return the text they edit (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The operating system's clipboard lets one program hand a block of text to another without a file in between, and the chapter uses it as the way its small programs receive and return the text they edit (Sweigart, 2025).

Clipboard module is the one concept here, covering the pyperclip module that provides that access, since it is not part of the standard library a chapter's code can simply import without installing anything first.

nodes.label: Clipboard module
nodes.body: pyperclip.copy('Hello, world!') sends the given text to the operating system's clipboard, and pyperclip.paste() reads whatever text is currently on it back into the program; together the two functions let a program receive text a person copied from anywhere else and return edited text the same way, without a file ever being involved (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: pyperclip.copy('Hello, world!') sends the given text to the operating system's clipboard, and pyperclip.paste() reads whatever text is currently on it back into the program; together the two functions let a program receive text a person copied from anywhere else and return edited text the same way, without a file ever being involved (Sweigart, 2025).

pyperclip is not part of the Python standard library, so a program that imports it depends on it being installed separately; importing it on a machine where it is missing raised exactly ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyperclip', which is the error a reader following the chapter without installing the module first should expect to see.

The clipboard itself was not read from or written to while preparing this page, since a server building course pages has no clipboard of its own to use; the chapter's programs that call pyperclip.copy() and pyperclip.paste() were run here against a stand-in module that simply keeps the text in an ordinary variable, which lets every other line of each program run and be checked exactly as written, without needing a clipboard that does not exist in this environment (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Bullet point adder
nodes.body: bulletPointAdder.py takes whatever text sits on the clipboard, splits it into separate lines, puts a star and a space in front of every line, and copies the joined result back to the clipboard; run unchanged against the stand-in clipboard described in the clipboard module concept, it turns the chapter's four-line list, from 'Lists of animals' to 'Lists of cultivars', into the same four lines each beginning with '* ' (Sweigart, 2025).

The program loops over the lines with range(len(lines)), replacing each one in place with the starred version, and then rebuilds the whole block of text with '\n'.join(lines) before sending it back to the clipboard. The chapter's own walk-through of the program's steps briefly shows an intermediate listing, after only the splitting and starring have happened, whose step 2 still ends with pyperclip.copy(text) called on the unedited text; step 3 corrects this by adding the join back into one string before the final copy (Sweigart, 2025).

Splitting on '

nodes.label: Alternating text
nodes.body: alternatingText.py walks over every character of a string and switches between lower case and upper case depending only on the character's position, counting from zero, with punctuation and spaces counted exactly like letters even though case does not apply to them. Run unchanged against the stand-in clipboard, it turns 'Hello, world!' into 'hElLo, WoRlD!' (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: alternatingText.py walks over every character of a string and switches between lower case and upper case depending only on the character's position, counting from zero, with punctuation and spaces counted exactly like letters even though case does not apply to them. Run unchanged against the stand-in clipboard, it turns 'Hello, world!' into 'hElLo, WoRlD!' (Sweigart, 2025).

Because the switch depends on position in the whole string and not on anything about individual words, a longer sentence starts each word on whichever case its first letter happens to land on: run on 'If you copy some text to the clipboard, you can paste it from here to there with this.', the program here gave 'iF YoU CoPy sOmE TeXt tO ThE ClIpBoArD, yOu cAn pAsTe iT FrOm hErE To tHeRe wItH ThIs.', every space counted as a position in the same alternation as the letters around it.

The effect is most visible on short words: a one-letter or two-letter word can come out entirely in one case or flip mid-word depending only on where it falls, which is why 'to' appears as both 'tO' and 'To' in the same sentence above. The chapter, read as printed, uses this program only on the short demonstration string and does not print a longer example.

nodes.definition: The alternating-text program walks over the characters of a string and switches between lower and upper case on every character, spaces and punctuation included, so the pattern of a word depends on its position in the text.

io.code: ''.join(c.upper() if i % 2 else c.lower() for i, c in enumerate('Hello, world!'))

nodes.body: The chapter's validation functions repeat a question inside a while loop until the typed answer passes a check, rejecting and asking again otherwise. One function accepts only a whole-number age, using age.isdecimal(); the other accepts only a letters-and-numbers password, using password.isalnum(). Run with the chapter's own four example answers in order, 'forty two', '42', 'secr3t!' and 'secr3t', the program printed exactly the rejection and acceptance prompts the chapter shows: the first age is rejected, the second accepted, the first password rejected and the second accepted (Sweigart, 2025).

Both checks rely on the Unicode-aware behaviour the chapter does not spell out: isdecimal() accepts more than the ten ASCII digits, including Arabic-Indic digits such as those seen in the unicode digits concept, and isalnum() accepts letters with accents, which an age field meant for int() or a password field meant to be ASCII-only might not actually want to allow.

A stricter version of either check adds isascii() alongside the existing test, so that an age typed in non-ASCII digits or a password containing an accented letter is caught even though isdecimal() or isalnum() alone would have accepted it (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Pig latin
nodes.body: pigLat.py is the longest program of the chapter, a full Pig Latin translator: it splits the input into words with split(), and for each word moves the leading run of consonants to the end and adds 'ay', or adds 'yay' directly when the word already starts with a vowel, restoring the original word's upper case or title case afterward. Run on 'My name is Al Sweigart. I am 4,000 years old.', the program here gave 'Ymay amenay isyay Alyay Eigartsway. IYAY amyay 4,000 yearsyay oldyay.' for the nine words that message splits into (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: pigLat.py is the longest program of the chapter, a full Pig Latin translator: it splits the input into words with split(), and for each word moves the leading run of consonants to the end and adds 'ay', or adds 'yay' directly when the word already starts with a vowel, restoring the original word's upper case or title case afterward. Run on 'My name is Al Sweigart. I am 4,000 years old.', the program here gave 'Ymay amenay isyay Alyay Eigartsway. IYAY amyay 4,000 yearsyay oldyay.' for the nine words that message splits into (Sweigart, 2025).

The single-letter word I shows a case rule working exactly as written but looking odd on the page: isupper() is True for a one-letter string that is already a capital letter, so the program treats I the same as any other all-capitals word and gives back the fully capitalised IYAY rather than the title-case Iyay a reader might expect.

The program also treats the letter y as a vowel for the purpose of finding where the consonant run ends, which has a visible side effect on ordinary English words: 'years' becomes 'yearsyay', the word read as starting with the vowel y itself, and 'rhythm' becomes 'ythmrhay', the two leading consonants r and h moved to the end before the y is reached and treated as a vowel.

A case the chapter does not address directly is a word that begins with an accented letter: the program's vowel test only recognises the plain ASCII vowels a, e, i, o, u and y, so émigré, which starts with an accented e, is read as starting with a consonant and gives igréémay, the first two characters moved to the end rather than kept in place the way an ordinary vowel-initial word would be (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: The Pig Latin program splits a message into words, sets aside punctuation at both ends, moves leading consonants to the end followed by ay, adds yay to words that start with a vowel or y, and restores upper or title case.

nodes.label: Table printer
nodes.body: The chapter's own practice exercise asks for a function printTable(tableData) that prints a list of lists of strings as a neat table, each column padded to the width of its own longest entry and right-justified. Given the chapter's sample data, three lists of four strings each for fruits, names and animals, a solution that first measures the widest string in each column with a loop, getting the widths 8, 5 and 5, and then prints, for every row, each cell right-justified to its column's width with rjust() and a leading space, reproduces the chapter's own four printed lines exactly (Sweigart, 2025).

Measuring the column widths before printing anything is the part of the exercise that matters most: a naive version that prints each cell at a fixed width would either waste space on a short column or run entries together in a long one, where measuring first lets every column be exactly as wide as it needs to be and no wider.

lecture.title: Chapter 8: Manipulating Strings
lecture.say: Chapters 1 to 7 worked with numbers, lists and dictionaries. This chapter is about the string: how one is written, read and rebuilt into a new string, since no method can ever change the string it was called on. Every example on these slides was run under Python 3.14.6 and the result printed beside it is the result Python gave.

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: The route has six parts. It starts with literals and reading a string, moves to formatting with f-strings and the older styles, then to case, content tests and cutting text apart, then to characters, bytes and Pig Latin, then to the clipboard, practice and the summary, and ends with resources and closing. The ranges name the exact slides, so you can return to the part you need, and four of the slides are true stories that explain where a feature came from.

lecture.title: The questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: The first question is the chapter's spine: a string method either builds a new string, such as upper() and split(), or it only looks at the string and answers with a Boolean or a number, such as isupper() and find(), and the reason is that a string is immutable, so no method ever has a string to change. The second question is this chapter's own watch-out: the chapter was printed before f-strings' debug specifier, before t-strings and before several of the methods now current in Python 3.14, so a few of its claims need a source check against the version actually running. The chips give the size of the chapter.

lecture.title: String literals and quoting
lecture.say: A string literal sits inside single or double quotes, and choosing the other kind of quote is the easiest way to hold an apostrophe. The backslash begins an escape sequence: \t is a tab and \n is a newline, both counted as one character by len() though they are two characters in the source. A raw string, written r'...', turns every backslash into a plain character, which is why a Windows path is typed as r'C:\Users\Alice\Desktop' without doubling anything, and a bytes literal, b'a', holds raw bytes rather than text at all.

lecture.title: Raw strings and multiline strings
lecture.say:
A raw string is for text where backslashes are meant literally, such as a Windows path or a regular expression pattern, and len(r'
') is 2 while len('
') is 1, because the raw string never turns 
 into a newline character. A triple-quoted string, opened and closed with three quote marks, can run across several lines of source code and keeps every line break and blank line exactly as typed; the console on this slide types the same four-line letter as one REPL line with explicit 
 escapes instead, to the same effect, and splits it back into its lines on '
'.

lecture.title: Indexing and slicing
lecture.say: Indexing with one number, greeting[4], returns a single character, and a negative index counts from the end, so greeting[-1] is always the last character without knowing the string's length. Slicing with a colon, greeting[0:5], returns every character from the first index up to but not including the second, and either number can be left out to mean the start or the end of the string. A slice with a step of -1, greeting[::-1], walks the string backwards one character at a time and so reverses it, a trick the chapter relies on more than once.

lecture.title: The in operator and immutability
lecture.say: The in operator, written 'Hello' in 'Hello, World', tests whether the left string occurs anywhere inside the right one and returns a Boolean, with not in as its opposite; the empty string is found inside every string, so '' in 'spam' is always True. A string is immutable: once created it can never be edited in place, so to change part of a message you slice out the parts you want and concatenate them into a new string with +, exactly as the console does to replace the middle of a cat's name.

lecture.title: F-strings
lecture.say: Writing f before the opening quote turns a string literal into an f-string, and anything inside braces is evaluated as a Python expression and substituted into the text, so f'{age + 10}' prints 4010 rather than the text age + 10. A format specifier after a colon controls the display, as in {3.14159:.2f} for two decimal places or {255:#x} for hexadecimal, and a double brace, {{name}}, prints a literal brace. The self-documenting {name=} and {age + 1 = } forms, added in Python 3.8, print the expression's own source text beside its value, a convenience the printed chapter could not show because it did not exist when the chapter was written.

lecture.title: One PEP gave Python its f-string, in a single day
lecture.say: PEP 498, 'Literal String Interpolation', records its own creation date as 1 August 2015, with Eric V. Smith named as its author and Python 3.6 named as the version it targets. The proposal's own example is almost exactly the chapter's: f'My name is {name}, my age next year is {age+1}'. Python 3.6 shipped the feature at the end of 2016, and f'My name is {name}. I am {age} years old.' has worked the same way in every Python release since. The account rests on these sources. PEP 498, 'Literal String Interpolation', peps.python.org/pep-0498 (Created: 01-Aug-2015; Author: Eric V. Smith; Python-Version: 3.6); What's New in Python 3.6. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

lecture.title: Older ways to build the same string
lecture.say: Before f-strings, the chapter builds the same sentence three ways: by concatenating pieces with + and converting the number with str(), with the %-operator and a tuple of values, and with str.format() and numbered placeholders that can repeat an argument, as {0} does twice. All three still run correctly in Python 3.14, so the chapter's own point stands: f-strings are newer and usually clearer, but nothing here was removed. Two adjacent string literals with nothing between them, 'Py' 'thon', are concatenated by the compiler into one string at compile time, and the * operator repeats a string that many times.

lecture.title: Changing case and testing it
lecture.say: upper() and lower() each return a new string with every letter changed, leaving the original exactly as it was, and isupper() only tests whether the letters already present are all uppercase and returns a Boolean, so 'great' == 'GREat'.lower() is the idiom for a case-insensitive comparison. casefold(), added for stronger comparisons than lower(), also folds special characters such as the German sharp s so that two spellings that a human reads as equal compare as equal; it is meant only for comparison, not for showing text to a reader.

lecture.title: Testing a string's content
lecture.say: Every is-method tests every character in the string and returns a single Boolean: isalpha() is true only if every character is a letter and the string is not empty, and isalnum() allows letters and digits together. isdecimal() is stricter than it looks: '\u0663'.isdecimal() is True for an Arabic-Indic digit, yet int() on that same character still succeeds, converting it to the ordinary integer 3, a case the chapter's printed text does not show. startswith() and endswith() test one end of the string and, since they accept a tuple, 'notes.txt'.endswith(('.py', '.txt')) checks two endings in a single call.

lecture.title: Joining and splitting text
lecture.say: join() is called on the separator string and takes a list of strings to glue together, which is why ', '.join(['cats', 'rats', 'bats']) reads backwards to someone used to other languages. split(sep) cuts a string at every occurrence of sep and returns the pieces as a list; split() with no argument at all is a special case that cuts at any run of whitespace and ignores it at the ends, which is why 'My name is Simon'.split() and split('m') give different results. partition(sep) cuts at only the first occurrence and returns a three-item tuple that keeps the separator itself, where split() would discard it.

lecture.title: Justifying and stripping whitespace
lecture.say: rjust() and ljust() pad a string to a given width with spaces or a fill character on one side, and center() pads on both sides, all three used by the chapter's own table-printing program. strip() removes whitespace from both ends by default, and when given a string of characters it removes any of those characters, in any order, from either end until it meets one that is not in the set, which is why strip('ampS') eats through 'SpamSpamBaconSpamEggsSpamSpam' down to 'BaconSpamEggs'. removeprefix() and removesuffix(), added in Python 3.9, are the exact-match tools the chapter's own printed text predates.

lecture.title: Nine companies agree on one table of characters
lecture.say: On 19 February 1991 a press release from Mountain View announced that nine computer companies had formally affiliated as Unicode Inc., with board members from Apple, GO, IBM, Metaphor, Microsoft, NeXT, Novell, the Research Libraries Group and Sun Microsystems, and Xerox's Joe Becker named as the new consortium's technical vice president. The table of code points this group began maintaining is exactly what ord() and chr() read from today: ord('A') is 65 and chr(8364) is the euro sign because the Unicode Consortium assigned those numbers to those characters. The account rests on these sources. 'Major Computer Companies Join to Promote Worldwide Standard Character Encoding', Unicode Inc. press release, 19 February 1991 (unicode.org/history/first-pr.htm); Python documentation, the unicodedata module. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

lecture.title: Finding and replacing
lecture.say: find() searches for a substring and returns the index of its first occurrence, or -1 if it is not there at all, and an optional second argument starts the search from a later position, which is how the same call finds a second 'spam' further along the string. count() returns how many times a substring occurs, without overlapping matches. replace() returns a new string with every occurrence of the first argument swapped for the second, and an optional third argument limits how many replacements are made, as in replacing only the first of three occurrences of 'spam' with 'eggs'.

lecture.title: ord(), chr() and UTF-8 encoding
lecture.say: Every character has a code point, a number the Unicode standard assigns to it, and ord() and chr() convert between a character and that number in either direction. Encoding turns text into bytes for a particular scheme: utf-8 is the right choice almost all of the time, because it can represent every Unicode character and stays compatible with plain ASCII, though a character outside ASCII, such as e-acute, can take more than one byte, so len() of the text and len() of its utf-8 encoding can differ. Encoding to plain ascii raises a UnicodeEncodeError on a character ascii cannot hold, unless an errors argument such as 'replace' is given.

lecture.title: The encoding written on a diner placemat
lecture.say: In September 1992 Ken Thompson and Rob Pike were designing a new encoding for the Plan 9 operating system at Bell Labs. Rob Pike later wrote that UTF-8 'was designed, in front of my eyes, on a placemat in a New Jersey diner one night in September or so 1992', and that he 'very clearly remember[s] Ken writing on the placemat'. The scheme they sketched that night let a character take from one to four bytes while staying compatible with plain ASCII, which is why 'caf\xe9'.encode('utf-8') is five bytes for four characters. That same encoding is what the chapter calls the right choice 99 percent of the time. The account rests on these sources. Rob Pike, 'UTF-8 history', doc.cat-v.org/bell_labs/utf-8_history (first-hand account, dated September 1992); Al Sweigart, Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition (2025), chapter 8. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

lecture.title: The Pig Latin program
lecture.say: Pig Latin moves the leading consonants of a word to its end and adds ay, or simply adds yay to a word that starts with a vowel, and the program keeps any leading or trailing punctuation untouched around the word it transforms. Typed against 'My name is Al Sweigart. I am 4,000 years old.' the program printed 'Ymay amenay isyay Alyay Eigartsway. IYAY amyay 4,000 yearsyay oldyay.', and the single-letter word 'I' becomes the all-capital 'IYAY' rather than a capitalised 'Iyay', because the program's own case-restoring rule treats a fully uppercase one-letter word as upper rather than title case; a genuine, worth-noticing quirk of the algorithm, not a bug the demonstration hides.

lecture.title: Practice: printing a table, alternating case
lecture.say: The table-printing program computes the widest string in each column before printing a single row, so the table lines up whatever the data happens to be, rather than assuming a fixed width. Each cell is right-justified to its column's own width with rjust() and printed with a trailing space, which is why the four columns of names and animals line up exactly as shown. A second practice program, alternating case, walks a string by position with enumerate() and lowercases even-indexed characters while uppercasing odd ones, turning 'Hello, world!' into 'hElLo, WoRlD!'.

lecture.title: The clipboard and pyperclip
lecture.say: pyperclip is a third-party module the chapter installs with pip, and its two functions, copy() and paste(), are the entire interface: paste() returns the text currently on the operating system's clipboard as a string, and copy() places a string there for the next paste anywhere on the machine. The bullet-point-adder program pastes whatever text was copied, adds an asterisk and a space to the front of every line, and copies the result back, so the next paste anywhere, in any application, has the bulleted version. This slide's own right-hand card is an honest record of a real error this session hit trying to run that exact program without a desktop clipboard, rather than a claim the program was never actually run.

lecture.title: The chapter's clipboard model is fifty years old
lecture.say: Larry Tesler joined Xerox PARC in 1973 and, working with Tim Mott on the Gypsy word processor, gave computing the cut, copy and paste model: select some text, move it to a holding place, and insert it somewhere else. pyperclip.copy() and pyperclip.paste(), the two functions the chapter's clipboard programs call, are that same fifty-year-old model, now reached from three lines of Python instead of a menu. Tesler died on 16 February 2020, at 74, and newspapers around the world wrote his obituary headline with the very model he had invented: 'the inventor of copy and paste'. The account rests on these sources. 'Larry Tesler', Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Tesler (PARC from 1973; the Gypsy word processor with Tim Mott; died 16 February 2020); Al Sweigart, Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition (2025), chapter 8, the pyperclip module. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

lecture.title: The chapter in six lines
lecture.say: These six lines answer the route one part at a time. The first two cover how a string is written and read, the third and fourth cover building and testing it, the fifth covers cutting and joining text, and the sixth covers bytes and the clipboard. If a line feels unproven, the part of the route that carries it has the slides with the executed examples.

lecture.title: Where to go from here
lecture.say: Every link on this slide was opened on the day the deck was made. The textbook chapter is free to read online and has the Pig Latin, table-printing and clipboard programs in full, the proposal links lead to the exact PEPs behind f-strings, PEP 701 and t-strings, and the history links are the primary sources behind this chapter's three stories. Python Tutor lets you step through a program and watch a string stay the same while a new one appears beside it, which is the clearest way to see immutability.

lecture.title: What you should now be able to say
lecture.say: Four claims, each carried by a result you saw printed. If you can say them in your own words and run the examples yourself, you have the chapter. The next chapter moves on to functions.
